name: Omar Rossi

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government, and we sell nothing. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal day at work look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead bike-share dock software at a tech company, where I am among the best at tracing false repair alerts. I use AI every day to draft tests but check them with mechanics’ logs. Seema makes metal racks, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us rent with fifteen months of expenses saved and many nearby tech firms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d tell the bike-share team that a little AI help can sort duplicate dock faults, but somebody still has to check whether a bicycle locks into the stand. I use AI every day to draft repair-alert tests and compare them with a mechanic’s dock log.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am 58, have a master’s degree and lead this software team at a tech company; I am one of the best here at finding false repair alerts. Seema makes metal racks for shops, our children are grown, and higher lead pay has helped us rent with fifteen months of expenses saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep checking one dock-failure report with the mechanic each Tuesday. We would put 280 monthly into our cash reserve while both incomes continue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel calm about our work and bills. A green dock light is useless if the bicycle rolls away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What failed at a dock?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The app said a bicycle was locked, but a bent latch let it move. I compared the mechanic’s inspection with the software event before we marked the dock safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why use AI daily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It drafts odd failure cases fast. I still check the latch report and run the test before a release.

say: I want **dock faults** checked against mechanic reports.
I use **AI daily** for draft alerts, then verify them.
think: I have **fifteen months saved** from higher lead pay and Seema’s metal-rack orders.
I see **rent covered** with our current incomes and fifteen-month reserve.
do: **Check dock failures** with a qualified mechanic each Tuesday before software release.
**Save 280 monthly** in cash reserve while both household incomes continue to arrive.
S0.quote: A green dock light is useless if the bicycle rolls away.
fieldNote: His **lead skill** comes from tracing software alerts to real latches, not claiming mechanic certification.
The **fifteen-month reserve** supports current rent without treating grown children’s wages as household income.

steps.text: Check one bike-share dock failure with mechanic each Tuesday
Save 280 monthly while developer pay and rack income continue

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say AI taking booking, checking and coding could write many dock alerts without us. I would keep a mechanic’s sign-off before the app tells a rider a bicycle is secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My lead hours could shrink if one engineer oversees automated repairs across the city. Fifteen months saved gives us time, but Seema’s rack sales alone would not replace my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d ask my manager for approved paid time to pilot a new AI dock-fault checker on retired stands, with a qualified mechanic reviewing each result. If approved, I’d test a bent latch weekly and keep logging real repairs while the current job pays; I would wait for staffing numbers before pursuing a different job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about my own hours but keen to test the checker. A model cannot feel a loose latch through a phone screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the mechanic review?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mechanic would tug the bicycle, record the latch movement and compare it with the tool’s warning. I would not let the checker clear a live dock from a test alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the pilot is refused?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep reviewing real dock logs and ask for written lead-hour plans. I would not call a private experiment a work tool.

say: I want **mechanic sign-off** before AI clears a dock.
I want **retired stands** used for paid tool testing.
think: I could lose **paid lead hours** across automated stations.
I have **fifteen months saved**, but not a guaranteed next wage.
do: **Pilot AI dock checker** weekly only with approved paid time, retired stands and qualified mechanic review.
**Keep logging real repairs** while developer role pays; wait for written staffing before changing jobs.
S1.quote: A model cannot feel a loose latch through a phone screen.
fieldNote: His **new AI pilot** goes beyond existing daily drafted tests and stays off live docks.
He keeps **current mechanic checks** while seeking staffing facts, without assuming another job is needed yet.

steps.text: Pilot AI checker on retired stands weekly with approved paid time and qualified mechanic review

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2028 could write bike-share code and schedule repairs cheaper than our team. Robots fixing physical bicycles and racks may follow around 2031, after our screen work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm could end my lead developer role, even with good fault records. Fifteen months saved is a substantial runway, but Seema’s workshop orders could not replace my steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d request written notice of lead cuts and keep four verified latch-failure cases that show what our software caught. If my job ends after 2028, I’d search paid local mobility-software vacancies only if they exist and wages cover our rent and bills; I would protect the cash reserve instead of buying repair machines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be alarmed at losing a wage I count on. Four true fault cases are evidence, not four job offers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you repair bicycles for pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after current safety training and a real paid opening. I know the logs, but the qualified mechanic knows the brakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave town for software work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would search nearby mobility and tech employers first. Seema’s rack customers and our rented home are here, so I am not planning a move.

say: I expect **AGI in 2028** to reach dock code first.
I expect **repair robots around 2031** to follow later.
think: I expect my **lead developer wage** could end when AGI writes dock code.
I know **fifteen months saved** buys a long search, not a replacement wage.
do: **Record four latch failures** and request written lead-cut notice while current job pays.
**Search mobility-software vacancies** after 2028 loss only if paid local openings cover rent and bills.
S2.quote: Four true fault cases are evidence, not four job offers.
fieldNote: He records **specific fault evidence** rather than buying repair equipment from savings.
The **local search** starts after job loss and requires real paid bill-covering openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say full AGI by 2031 gives us time to find out which dock problems a person still has to see on site. Robots fixing bicycles may follow around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could test whether small venue operators will pay for clear dock-access notes while my developer wage lasts. Fifteen months saved lets me try one bounded project, but I would not count on demand before a client signs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d offer one paid dock-access survey to a local cycling club only if it signs an order, the bike-share operator permits access and my employer approves outside work. I’d use my current phone, require the club to cover travel and leave at least twelve months of expenses untouched; we would save 260 monthly while both incomes hold, and after 2031 developer job loss I’d seek paid local mobility-software openings only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d be anxious about the code role but interested in a small paid test. A signed order tells me more than ten friendly conversations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the club receive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would record the dock location, step-free path and visible latch faults, with photographs the operator permits. I would not certify a bicycle as mechanically safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the operator refuses access?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not enter the site or take the club’s money. I would keep the developer wage and look for another permitted paid project.

I expect **repair robots around 2034** to follow later.
think: I can test **one paid project** while lead pay lasts.
I need **signed demand** and twelve months saved before spending time on it.
do: **Survey paid club dock** only with signed order, operator access, employer approval, owned phone, covered travel and twelve-month reserve.
**Seek paid mobility software** after 2031 loss only if local vacancies cover rent and bills.
feel: **Anxious but testing** a bounded paid project.
S3.quote: A signed order tells me more than ten friendly conversations.
fieldNote: His **side project** needs a paying client, site permission, outside-work approval and protected reserve.
The **future job search** remains conditional on software displacement and bill-covering local vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d say ten years before full AGI in 2036 gives us room to improve dock records and test whether small clubs value field notes. Robots repairing bikes and racks may follow around 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may still want paid work at 68 and have not verified a retirement amount. Our fifteen-month reserve makes the next few years secure, but future club contracts cannot be counted before they are signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d keep maintaining dock software and save 270 monthly while both incomes hold. I’d take at most two paid club surveys a quarter only with signed orders, operator access, employer outside-work approval, travel covered and twelve months of expenses untouched; if the developer job ends after 2036, I’d search paid local mobility-software vacancies only if wages cover rent and bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I’d feel uneasy about a later job change but secure now. A small paid survey is a test of demand, not a retirement business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy survey equipment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use the phone I own and decline work needing machinery. A signed client still does not justify risking our rent reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children join the project?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have their own work and households. Seema and I will plan from real paid orders, not their labour.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my lead wage could end before another paid local mobility opening exists. Written notice and a real bill-covering vacancy would help us use the reserve deliberately.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn’t ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask whether a cycling club’s interest means I have a business. I would not call a club conversation income before a signed order and site permission.

headlineQuote: I would not call a club conversation income before a signed order and site permission.

He and Seema **rent** while their grown children live separately.
He **uses AI daily** but verifies dock alerts with mechanics.
He tests **paid club surveys** only with signed demand, operator access, employer approval, covered travel and protected savings.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end his lead wage before paid local mobility work appears.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and a real local bill-covering vacancy would help.
